title: Storing Billions of Short Links
prompt: A link shortener turns long web addresses into short codes such as `sho.rt/aB3kZ9q`. Opening a short link looks up its code and redirects. Design how the links are stored across servers.
facts: About 3 billion links, about 500 bytes each, and about 2,000 new links per second
Peak: about 200,000 link lookups per second; every lookup includes the code
Codes are 7 random characters, so new codes are spread evenly over all possible codes
Measured: one shard (a leader with two read replicas) holds about 500 GB and serves about 25,000 lookups per second and 5,000 writes per second safely
Target: plan for twice today's links and lookups without a full reshuffle of the data
scope: Creating codes and analytics are out of scope

requirements: States the lookup load, the storage, and that growth to twice the size must not move all the data
estimation: Storage: 3 × 10⁹ × 500 bytes = 1.5 TB ÷ 500 GB = 3 shards; lookups: 200,000 ÷ 25,000 = 8 shards; writes: 2,000 ÷ 5,000 needs less than 1; so 8 shards, about 16 when the size doubles
design: Shards partitioned by the code, with the app finding a code's shard from the code alone
data: A partition key of the code, since every lookup includes it
Growth without moving everything: consistent hashing with virtual nodes, or range partitioning by code with ranges that are split when they grow
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: hash mod N would move about 8 in 9 links when a ninth shard is added; range splits need a step that moves half of one range at a time; a viral link is a hot key but reads of one code are served by that shard's replicas (or a cache, SD 3)

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, consistent hashing: the code is hashed onto a ring with about 100 virtual nodes per shard. Storage needs 1.5 TB ÷ 500 GB = 3 shards and lookups 200,000 ÷ 25,000 = 8, so 8 shards, each with a leader and two read replicas. Doubling to 16 shards adds servers one at a time, and each new one takes about 1/(N+1) of the links from all the others. Trade-off: a very popular link is read from one shard's replicas; a cache in front can take that load.

Design B, range partitioning by code: because codes are random, 8 equal code ranges get equal load (200,000 ÷ 8 = 25,000 lookups each). When a range grows past 500 GB or 25,000 lookups per second, it is split in two and half moves to a new server, so growth to 16 shards moves one range at a time. Trade-off: a directory of ranges must be kept and read by the app, and splits must be planned.

assumptions: Lookups are spread evenly over codes, apart from a few popular links
Each shard keeps its own replicas and backups
reference.design:
Links are hash-partitioned by their code with consistent hashing and about 100 virtual nodes per shard. Every lookup includes the code, so it reads exactly one shard.
Size: 3 × 10⁹ × 500 bytes = 1.5 TB, 3 shards' worth; lookups: 200,000 ÷ 25,000 = 8 shards; writes need less than one. So 8 shards today, each a leader with two read replicas.
Growth: doubling to 16 shards means adding servers one at a time; each new one takes about 1/(N+1) of the links, a little from every shard, instead of the 8 in 9 that hash mod N would move.
A viral link stays on one shard, whose replicas, and a cache if needed, serve it.
alternatives: Range partitioning by code: works because codes are random, with planned range splits
Rejected: hash mod N, because adding a shard moves most links

title: Readings from 100,000 Sensors
prompt: A company collects temperature readings from 100,000 sensors in buildings. Users look at one sensor's readings over the last day, and a nightly job computes hourly averages for every sensor. Design how the readings are stored across servers.
facts: Each sensor sends one reading every 10 seconds; a reading takes about 100 bytes
Readings are kept for one year
Measured: one shard holds about 4 TB and takes about 3,000 writes per second safely
Target: a one-sensor, one-day query reads one shard; storage and write limits hold for the whole year
Sensor ids are assigned in order as sensors are installed, and new buildings add about 10,000 sensors a year
scope: Storing readings and the two queries
Alerts and dashboards are out of scope

requirements: States the write rate, the one-year retention and that one sensor's day of readings must come from one shard
estimation: Storage: 10,000 × 100 bytes × 86,400 × 365 ≈ 31.5 TB a year ÷ 4 TB ≈ 7.9, so 8 shards; storage wins
design: Shards partitioned by sensor, so one sensor's readings stay together, ordered by time within the shard
data: A partition key of the sensor id (hashed, or in ranges that stay balanced as sensors are added), with readings ordered by time inside the shard
Explains why partitioning by time alone would put all 10,000 writes per second on the newest shard
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: the nightly job reads every shard (scatter-gather), which is acceptable at night; ranges of sensor ids put all new sensors on the last shard, so they must be split or hashed; old readings could be deleted after a year by dropping old data per shard

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, hash by sensor id: 10,000 writes per second need 4 shards, but 31.5 TB a year needs 8, so 8 shards with consistent hashing. One sensor's day is about 8,640 readings on one shard, ordered by time. The nightly job reads all 8 shards in parallel. Trade-off: no range of sensor ids lives on one shard, which nobody needs here.

Design B, ranges of sensor ids: 8 ranges of 12,500 sensors each (about 4 TB a year and 1,250 writes per second per shard). Because new sensors get the highest ids, the last range grows; it is split when it passes 12,500 sensors, so about one split a year for 10,000 new sensors. Trade-off: splits must be planned, but a building's sensors, installed together, stay on one shard.

assumptions: The nightly job may take an hour
reference.design:
Readings are partitioned by a hash of the sensor id, with consistent hashing, and stored by sensor and time inside each shard.
Writes: 100,000 sensors ÷ 10 s = 10,000 readings per second, which 4 shards could take. Storage: 10,000 × 100 bytes × 86,400 × 365 ≈ 31.5 TB a year, which needs 8 shards of 4 TB. So 8 shards.
A one-sensor, one-day query (about 8,640 readings) reads one shard. The nightly averages job reads all 8 shards in parallel, a scatter-gather that is fine at night.
Partitioning by time would send all 10,000 writes per second to the newest shard.
alternatives: Ranges of sensor ids with planned splits: keeps a building's sensors together
Rejected: partitioning by time, because the newest shard would take all writes
